method: The Hebrew calendar is a fixed arithmetic calendar, so a Hebrew date is a pure function of the year and needs no observation. Each 19-year cycle holds twelve common years and seven leap years: year y is leap when (7y + 1) mod 19 is less than 7, and a leap year carries thirteen months by inserting Adar I (30 days) before Adar II (29 days). Days are counted from a fixed epoch. The months elapsed since year 1 are 235 per completed cycle, plus 12 per regular year of the current cycle, plus the leap months of that cycle; the molad of Tishrei then follows from 29 days, 12 hours and 793 parts per month, and the four dehiyyot postpone Rosh Hashanah by at most two days. The first defers a molad at or after midday (18 hours from the start of the Hebrew day at 6 pm). The second defers a Tuesday molad at or after 9 hours and 204 parts in a common year, the third a Monday molad at or after 15 hours and 589 parts at the end of a leap year, and the fourth a Sunday, Wednesday or Friday that would otherwise be 1 Tishrei. The resulting year is 353, 354 or 355 days when common and 383, 384 or 385 when leap, which is what fixes Cheshvan at 29 or 30 days (30 only in a complete year) and Kislev at 29 or 30 (30 except in a deficient year); Tishrei, Shevat, Nisan, Sivan and Av always keep 30 days and Tevet, Iyar, Tammuz, Elul and Adar II 29. Both directions go through one continuous day count shared with the Gregorian calendar, so the weekday is that count modulo 7 and the two calendars cannot drift apart. Adar I exists only in leap years and Adar II only in leap years too, so a month that the chosen year does not have is refused, and a day beyond the month's length is refused with the length that month has in that year. Civil dates from 1600-01-01 to 2200-12-31 are supported, Hebrew years 5360 to 5961, and a Hebrew date whose civil day falls outside that window is refused. The result is the Hebrew date in force during the daylight hours of the civil date entered, because a Hebrew day begins at sunset, so the evening before already belongs to the next Hebrew date; no time of day or location is taken. Everything is calculated in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.
